On This Day — August 31, 1945

A version of journalist Leslie Nakashima’s eyewitness report from Hiroshima ran in The New York Times, one of the first accounts of the atomic bomb’s devastation to reach American readers, and one of the first to be publicly contradicted by the same paper that printed it.

Nakashima was born in Hawaii and had spent the war years in Tokyo as a correspondent for United Press. When Japan surrendered, he boarded a train to find his mother, who lived on the outskirts of Hiroshima. Sixteen days after the bomb fell, he arrived to find the city’s station in ruins, with nothing left standing between him and the mountains in the distance.

His mother survived. The city she lived near did not. In his dispatch, Nakashima wrote plainly that what had been a city of 300,000 population had vanished, and estimated the death toll would reach 100,000.

His full dispatch went further than most Americans ever saw. He described warnings that uranium had seeped into the ground and that the city might be uninhabitable for 75 years, according to Japanese authorities. Many newspapers cut that out. The New York Times ran its version on August 31, keeping only a single line, that people continued to die daily from burns suffered from the bomb’s ultra-violet rays, before inserting a rebuttal directly beneath it: “United States scientists say the atomic bomb will not have lingering after-effects in a devastated area.” Those scientists were tied to the Manhattan Project, the same government program that built the bomb Nakashima had just watched erase a city.

History often credits Australian journalist Wilfred Burchett as the first to expose Hiroshima’s true toll. But Nakashima’s report came more than a week earlier. The truth was there all along. It was just published next to a denial of itself.

He described warnings that uranium had seeped into the ground and that the city might be uninhabitable for 75 years, according to Japanese authorities. Many newspapers cut that out. The New York Times ran its version on August 31, keeping only a single line, that people continued to die daily from burns suffered from the bomb’s ultra-violet rays, before inserting a rebuttal directly beneath it: “United States scientists say the atomic bomb will not have lingering after-effects in a devastated area.” Those scientists were tied to the Manhattan Project, the same government program that built the bomb Nakashima had just watched erase a city.

History often credits Australian journalist Wilfred Burchett as the first to expose Hiroshima’s true toll. But Nakashima’s report came more than a week earlier. The truth was there all along. It was just published next to a denial of itself.
